result.summary: Pausanias tells how Lycaon founded Lycosura and the cult of Lycæan Zeus, contrasting him with Cecrops. Lycaon sacrificed a baby and became a wolf, which Pausanias accepts as an old tradition. He argues that in the early age gods and men mingled, and warns that falsehood is often grafted onto true marvels.

scenes.title: Lycaon's foundations and festivals
scenes.summary: Lycaon founds Lycosura and the Lycæa; Pausanias compares this with the Pan-Athenæa and Olympic games and dates Lycaon alongside Cecrops.

scenes.title: Cecrops' cakes, Lycaon's sacrifice
scenes.summary: Cecrops offers only cakes, while Lycaon sacrifices a baby to Lycæan Zeus and is turned into a wolf.
scenes.stakes: Lycaon risks the wrath of the god for his impious murder and loses his human form.

scenes.title: Pausanias on gods and marvels
scenes.summary: Pausanias argues early men were rewarded or punished by gods, cites mortals made gods, and cautions against exaggerated tales such as werewolf festivals and weeping Niobe.

alias_notes.explanation: Zeus as worshipped on Mount Lycæus, a cult title.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias warns that loving marvels leads people to mix fiction with truth and lose credibility.

analysis.text: Piety and impiety are rewarded or punished by the gods, and Lycaon's wolf-change shows divine wrath on human crime.
Pausanias is a rationalising traveller who accepts old local traditions yet distrusts embellished marvels, and he sees his own age as morally declined.

legacy.text: The Lycaon wolf-man tale is a source of the word lycanthropy and of later werewolf lore.

fun_facts.text: Mount Lykaion's ash altar of Zeus has been excavated, and finds there include ancient votive offerings.

language_notes.text: Pan-Athenæa was Athens' great festival of all Athenians; Pausanias argues the name only arose after Theseus united the Attic towns into one city.
Athenians claimed Olympic origins in myth: Cronos and Zeus wrestled, and the Curetes (divine attendants of infant Zeus) ran the first race. Pausanias declines to discuss this here.
Pelanoi were cakes or meal-offerings made without animal sacrifice; the Greek term is given here as _pelani_.
"Guests at the tables of the gods" means that in the early age gods and righteous men dined together familiarly.
Tritons were sea-beings, part human and part fish; the shell is a conch-like trumpet, so the story explains their "voice" as shell-sound.

context_notes.text: Lycaon was an early king of Arcadia; Lycosura was reputed one of the oldest cities, and the Lycæa was an Arcadian festival of Zeus.
Cecrops was the legendary first king of Athens, half-man and half-serpent in many accounts.
Aristæus, Britomartis, Hercules, Amphiaraus, Castor and Pollux were all figures worshipped as gods or heroes though said to have been born mortal.
Niobe boasted of her many children against Leto; her children were slain and she was turned to weeping stone on Mount Sipylus.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias contrasts Cecrops' restraint with Lycaon's brutality, using their piety toward Zeus to define each as wise or impious.
The author speaks in the first person as a cautious judge, accepting some traditions as plausible while weighing others.
Pausanias laments his own age: gods no longer make mortals divine except through flattery, and punishment comes only after death.
Pausanias closes with a general moral: love of wonder leads listeners to exaggerate and so discredit true accounts.
